title: Clock and Regiment
premise: In 1913 London, Orsen Winterbourne serves as driver and courier to the suffragist Marchmont household, quietly reading every letter that passes through their hands. When a sealed dispatch reveals the family is being framed for a bombing they did not commit, Orsen must decide whether to stay invisible or act, drawing on a found family of printers, seamstresses, and a disgraced police clerk to uncover who is forging evidence against them. As the workshop that shelters their network faces demolition orders and the trial date closes in, Orsen races to deliver the truth to the one person who can stop it. The story ends with justice won outside the courtroom—through testimony smuggled in plain sight—and Orsen finally claiming a name, a home, and a family of their own.
about_author: Theo Amberdale is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing letters from the British suffrage movement before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about the people history forgot to name.

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. We meet them measuring parcels in the Marchmont household, reading letters by lamplight before delivery—a habit born of protecting the family, never betraying them. Establishes the workshop below stairs where the network prints pamphlets. Emotional beat: quiet belonging inside deliberate invisibility.

chapters.title: Orders Come at Dusk
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine run to a printer's alley turns tense when police watch the street; Orsen memorizes faces and routes. Mrs. Marchmont gives her first hint she suspects her driver reads what shouldn't be read. Emotional beat: the first crack in Orsen's careful anonymity.

chapters.title: Sealed in Wax
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A letter arrives with an unfamiliar seal; inside, a threat naming the Marchmonts in a bombing plot scheduled to be 'discovered' within weeks. Orsen must choose: burn it, or break every rule of invisibility. Emotional beat: dread hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Household That Isn't Mine
chapters.summary: Daughter Cressida Marchmont's POV. She notices Orsen's sleeplessness and confronts them gently; Orsen deflects but nearly tells all. Cressida reveals she's been followed too. Emotional beat: two guarded people recognizing each other as allies.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen inventories the workshop—presses, type, ledgers—deciding what can be moved if the raid comes. They recruit Nell, a seamstress who sews documents into coat linings. Emotional beat: fear transformed into methodical preparation.

chapters.title: A Clerk Without a Badge
chapters.summary: Disgraced police clerk Ambrose Pell's POV. Pell, dismissed for refusing to falsify a report, recognizes the forgery techniques in leaked case notes. He approaches Orsen through the printer's alley. Emotional beat: wary trust between two people burned by institutions.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Fingernails
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Pell traces the forged evidence to a private firm hired by someone inside the Home Office; the trail points to a man named Halloway. Meanwhile the demolition order on the workshop is posted. Emotional beat: the conspiracy acquires a face and a clock.

chapters.title: Sunday Dinner, Loaded Silence
chapters.summary: Cressida's POV. The Marchmonts host allies for Sunday dinner while Orsen serves; coded conversation passes plans across the table. Mr. Marchmont learns of the frame and refuses to flee. Emotional beat: the family choosing to stand rather than scatter.

chapters.title: The Long Road to Birmingham
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A driving run to contact a sympathetic journalist becomes a chase when a tail follows them north. Orsen loses the tail in fog using roads learned from years of deliveries. Emotional beat: competence under pressure; loneliness briefly lifted by success.

chapters.title: Nell's Needles
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell hides the original threatening letter and copied forgeries into garments bound for a safehouse, reflecting on how sewing—women's invisible work—becomes resistance. Emotional beat: pride in craft as weapon.

chapters.title: Halloway Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Halloway corners Orsen privately, offering money and immunity to hand over the workshop's ledgers. Orsen pretends to consider, buying time and learning the raid is set for ten days hence. Emotional beat: terror masked as composure.

chapters.title: The Ledger Problem
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. The ledgers contain names of everyone in the network; if seized, dozens fall with the Marchmonts. Pell proposes copying and dispersing them, but a copyist is needed whom no one will suspect. Emotional beat: the cost of protection made concrete.

chapters.title: Cressida Breaks a Rule
chapters.summary: Cressida's POV. Impatient with secrecy, Cressida contacts the journalist directly and is nearly caught; Orsen extracts her, and the two argue bitterly about risk and trust. Emotional beat: fracture in the found family, then reluctant reconciliation.

chapters.title: Ten Days
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A countdown chapter: pages copied at night, routes rehearsed, the press dismantled piece by piece and hidden in a hearse Orsen borrows. Each day ends with a line marking time lost. Emotional beat: mounting pressure rendered in ritual.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Vanished
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Their key witness—a former forger at Halloway's firm—disappears the night before deposition. Pell suspects a leak and turns suspicion inward, straining the group. Emotional beat: paranoia threatening the alliance.

chapters.title: Smoke Over the Alley
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Fire guts the printer's alley two days early—not the raid, but arson meant to destroy evidence. Nell saves the type and a scorched ledger page proving Halloway's watermark. Emotional beat: loss sharpening purpose.

chapters.title: What the Watermark Said
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. The recovered page matches paper stock sold only to Halloway's office. Pell drafts an affidavit knowing it ends his career permanently. Emotional beat: sacrifice accepted without ceremony.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Police arrive at the empty workshop; Orsen stalls Inspector Dane with tea and paperwork while the last crate leaves through the coal chute. Dane, unconvinced but unpersuaded, lets them go with a warning. Emotional beat: nerve held to the final second.

chapters.title: Delivered by Hand
chapters.summary: Cressida's POV. The affidavit reaches the journalist and, through him, a reformist MP who forces the Home Office to suspend proceedings. Halloway's firm is exposed; the vanished witness resurfaces in protective custody, having fled the fire. Emotional beat: vindication arriving not in court but in print.

chapters.title: Halloway's Quiet End
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Halloway resigns rather than face inquiry, his patron abandoning him; justice outside the law proves colder and more complete than any trial. Pell declines reinstatement, choosing the network instead. Emotional beat: bittersweet triumph.

chapters.title: A Name of One's Own
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Mrs. Marchmont formally offers Orsen a partnership in the reconstituted press, and Orsen signs a document—the first they haven't read secretly—for the first time as an equal. Emotional beat: invisibility exchanged for chosen visibility.

chapters.title: Clock and Regiment
chapters.summary: Ensemble close, Orsen's POV anchoring. Months later, the new press runs its first edition; the found family gathers—Marchmonts, Nell, Pell, Cressida—as Orsen locks the door and carries nothing but keys. Final beat: memory kept, justice kept, home kept.
